L2@P0: Maps between local Picard groups
L3@P0: J´anos Koll´ar
L4@P0: Abstract
L5@P0: The paper investigates maps between local Picard groups. The main goal is to understand the kernel in two cases: pull-back to the normalization and restriction to a hyperplane section. We give sufficient (and almost necessary) conditions that guarantee
L6@P0: that the kernel is finite or of finite type.
L7@P0: 1. Introduction
L8@P0: Let X be a scheme and x ∈ X a point. The local Picard group of X at x, denoted by Picloc(x, X),
L9@P0: is the Picard group of the punctured neighborhood SpecX Ox,X \ {x}. Our aim is to study the
L10@P0: pull-back map on the local Picard group in two situations.
L11@P0: Question 1.1 (Normalization). Let π : X¯ → X denote the normalization, and let ¯xi ∈ X¯ be the
L12@P0: preimages of x. What is the kernel of the pull-back map

L24@P0: In both cases we are interested in conditions that guarantee that the kernels of these maps are
L25@P0: “small”. Here “small” can mean trivial, or finite, or “naturally” a subgroup of a linear algebraic
L26@P0: group.
L27@P0: Grothendieck’s local Lefschetz-type theorem [Gro68, XI.3.16] is the first major result on
L28@P0: Question 1.2. He proves that r

L31@P0: that this can be relaxed to depthx X > 3 and dim X > 4. This was proved in [Kol13a] when X
L32@P0: is log canonical and in [BdJ14] when X is normal.
L33@P0: I was led to Question 1.1 while investigating stable varieties and their moduli. The method
L34@P0: of [Kol13b] first studies the normalization X¯ of a stable variety X and then descends the information from X¯ to X. It is especially important to know when the canonical divisor of X is
L35@P0: Q-Cartier; this was settled in [Kol11]. For semi-log canonical varieties Question 1.1 is answered
L36@P0: in [Kol13b, Section 5.7].

L46@P1: In many applications, the natural assumption is that X satisfies Serre’s condition S2 only. To
L47@P1: understand this case, one needs to know that, as in the global situation, the local Picard group
L48@P1: is not just a group but a group scheme. The local definition is more involved than the projective
L49@P1: one, and the natural setting turns out to be the following.
L50@P1: Condition 1.3. We consider a scheme X that is essentially of finite type over a field k, and
L51@P1: a 0-dimensional closed subscheme x ⊂ X. The scheme X satisfies Serre’s condition S2 and has
L52@P1: pure dimension at least 3 (that is, every associated prime of OX has the same dimension, which
L53@P1: is at least 3).
L54@P1: Boutot [Bou78] defines a local Picard functor Picloc(x, X) and proves that, under the above
L55@P1: assumptions, it is represented by the local Picard scheme Picloc(x, X); see Definition 3.3 and
L56@P1: [Bou78, Theorem 1.ii] for details. Frequently, Picloc(x, X) has infinitely many connected components. The identity component, usually denoted by Picloc−◦(x, X), is a commutative, connected
L57@P1: algebraic group of finite type, but it need not be a linear algebraic group. The union of those components of Picloc(x, X) that become torsion modulo Picloc−◦(x, X) is denoted by Picloc−τ
L58@P1: (x, X).
